summary.text: The model treats a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: for a typical patient, it goes from about 20% at 0 vessels to about 96% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 83%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 20%) (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher serum cholesterol as raising the predicted risk of heart disease steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 12% at 193 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L) to about 40% at 308 mg/dL (8.0 mmol/L) (on the training data only).

A higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than an upsloping ST segment (quickly at first, then levelling off for patients with slope of the ST segment at peak exercise other than an upsloping ST segment): for a typical patient, resting blood pressure going from 110 mm Hg to 155 mm Hg moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 72% to about 88% if slope of the ST segment at peak exercise is something other than an upsloping ST segment, and from about 17% to about 25% if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise.

Through one part of the model, age only lowers the predicted risk of heart disease once it rises above about 59 years: for a typical such patient, going from 29 years to 68 years moves it from about 20% to about 14% (on the training data only).
